This comes despite the typical family debt load remaining unchanged since 2022, suggesting that more households are struggling to keep up with existing financial obligations.

"If I have a one-on-one with you and you tell me there's a problem and we debate it and we say, 'Here's the solution,' we haven't consulted anyone else. So now we just made a decision and no one else helped, consulted, or knew how we made that decision."

"'Hire great people, trust them, let them do their job, stay out of the details, do recurring one-on-ones.' I don't believe any of that, and I wanna acknowledge that many great leaders do."

On my recent piece:

I read this generous critique with interest, but I suspect that the central argument of my analysis has not been fully understood. Huntington’s Clash of Civilizations rests on a fundamental premise: that Western civilization remains sufficiently coherent, self-assured, and conscious of its own identity to recognize itself as engaged in a civilizational confrontation with another.

My contention, informed in part by personal experience, is that Western civilization, or perhaps more precisely its European and U.S. expressions, is itself undergoing a profound crisis of identity and confidence. Civilizations in such a condition often lose the capacity to distinguish their own struggles from those of others. They become susceptible to internalizing external antagonisms, gradually transforming foreign conflicts into domestic ones.

Islam, meanwhile, is engaged in an intense struggle within itself, between competing theological, political, and civilizational visions. I believe these internal antagonisms will deepen over the coming decades. The more consequential question, however, is what happens when a Western civilization already beset by its own existential uncertainties becomes entangled in these struggles, absorbing them into its political and intellectual life.

This is where my analysis departs most fundamentally from Huntington. The defining civilizational confrontation of our time may not be one between a confident West and an external Islamic civilization, but one in which a fractured West increasingly becomes the arena in which the internal conflicts of another civilization are fought.

Book recommendation:

Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, Turgenev, Chekhov, and many others read Goncharov’s Oblomov and Lenin repeatedly invoked Oblomov in his writings and speeches as  the ultimate symbol of Russian inertia. Unfortunately, I don’t think this novel receives nearly the recognition it deserves. In my eyes, it’s the greatest Russian novel ever written.

There’s something eternal about it. The tension between grand aspirations and complete passivity, the seductions of opulence, the inability to act even when one knows perfectly well what must be done. There are echoes of it in French literature, particularly in Flaubert’s Bouvard et Pécuchet and Huysmans’s À rebours, where retreat from the world and the pursuit of an ideal existence become their own forms of imprisonment.

Although Goncharov was writing about distinctly Russian problems, I’ve always found something profoundly late-imperial/something recurrent about Oblomov. A society so accustomed to comfort, so absorbed in its habits and fantasies, that it gradually loses the will to act. 

More importantly, what makes the novel so captivating is how easily one can understand Oblomov’s desires. Who hasn’t imagined a life in which comfort, leisure, and freedom from obligation are the ultimate goals? But what happens when the very comfort you spend your life pursuing ends up eating you alive?

Royalty is a very simple concept, paying a fixed % out of the revenue top line 

Royalties already work in the IP world and many similar industries

Imagine instead of buying Apple stock where you gotta reason about their entire balance sheet, you could buy a iphone 18 royalty claim, giving you the % royalty from lifetime iphone 18 sales

Now bring it on-chain where all the revenue streams would live and thus enable programmable royalty

I do believe this would be very popular concept for retail to invest in, given how simple it is to understand

Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

Perhaps what remains is awareness itself.
